title: The forest years

segments.voice: Yesterday: paduka, Rama's sandals on a throne Bharata wouldn't take. Not mine. Now the three in the forest settle in.

Start with what they left. A prince who grew up with servants and elephants. A princess who wore silk. A brother who rode in chariots beside him. Now: a hut of leaves and branches that Lakshmana built by hand, on a hill called Chitrakoot, beside a river. They wear bark cloth, eat fruit and roots, and bathe in the river at dawn. Rama points out the trees and birds to Sita, the flowers on the hillside, the elephants coming down to drink. For a while, this is the whole story. No battles. No palace. And the strange thing is, in the text, they're happy.
screen: `A HUT OF LEAVES.` → `BARK, FRUIT, A RIVER AT DAWN.` → `THEY'RE HAPPY.`

segments.voice: After Bharata's visit they move deeper south, into the great Dandaka forest, and meet the sages who live in the woods. The sage Atri and his wife Anasuya, a holy woman famous for her devotion, who welcomes Sita like a daughter and gives her gifts and advice. The sage Agastya, who gives Rama divine weapons. The text says they spent about ten years moving from one hermitage to another, learning, listening, living simply. Eventually they settle at Panchavati, by the Godavari river. Today's word: vanaprastha. Vana means forest; vanaprastha is the one who goes to the forest. It's one of the four stages of life in Hindu tradition. First, the student. Second, the householder: work, family, raising children. Third, vanaprastha: when your children have children, you step back from the business of the world and turn toward the inner life. Fourth, the renouncer, who lets go of everything. Traditionally the forest stage comes late. Rama is too young for it; he's there by exile, not by age. But those years look a lot like it. Fewer things. Fewer roles. More attention. When almost everything was taken away, what was left turned out to be enough. One syllable holds it: less.
screen: `INTO THE DANDAKA FOREST.` · `ATRI, ANASUYA, AGASTYA.` · `VANAPRASTHA — TO THE FOREST.` · `THE FOUR STAGES OF LIFE.` · then, large: `LESS.`

segments.voice: If you can, put your phone face down or out of reach, and sit with nothing in your hands. Don't plan or fix anything; just notice what's here, your breath, the air on your skin, the sounds around you, like the river at Chitrakoot. For these two minutes you need nothing else; see if that's true.
Vanaprastha. The forest-dweller: the third stage of life, when you step back from the world and turn inward.
Your line: less. A hut of leaves by a river, and they were happy. Day forty-five, done.

howItsDone: Hindu tradition describes four stages of life (student, householder, forest-dweller, renouncer); today some older Hindus take up a simpler, more devotional life in the spirit of vanaprastha, and Chitrakoot and Panchavati are pilgrimage places.

chat.says: How could Rama and Sita be happy in a leaf hut after losing a palace?
options: With fewer things and roles, they had more attention, and what was left was enough.
The forest sages gave them gold and servants to replace what they lost.
They knew the exile would only last a few months, so it felt like a holiday.
chat.meaning: In the forest they lived simply: fewer things, fewer roles, more attention. What was left turned out to be enough.
